reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma arises from the epithelium of the nasopharynx, most often in the fossa of Rosenmuller, and shows a strong association with Epstein-Barr virus and with certain geographic and dietary factors
A very common presentation is a painless neck lump from cervical nodal metastasis, which may be the first and only sign
Unilateral serous otitis media with hearing loss in an adult should raise strong suspicion, as the tumour blocks the Eustachian tube opening
Nasal symptoms include blockage and blood-stained nasal or postnasal discharge
Skull base and cavernous sinus invasion can cause cranial nerve palsies, producing diplopia, facial numbness or other neurological deficits
Because the tumour hides in the nasopharynx, diagnosis relies on endoscopic examination and biopsy, supported by imaging and Epstein-Barr virus serology or DNA levels
MRI best defines local and skull base extension while CT and PET assess bony involvement and distant spread
Treatment is primarily radiotherapy, often with concurrent chemotherapy, because the tumour is radiosensitive and surgery has a limited primary role
reference.pathophysiology: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma develops in the epithelial lining of the nasopharynx, typically in the recess of the fossa of Rosenmuller near the Eustachian tube opening. Malignant transformation is closely linked to latent Epstein-Barr virus infection, together with genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures such as diets rich in preserved salted foods and nitrosamines. The tumour tends to spread submucosally and infiltrate early, obstructing the Eustachian tube to cause middle ear effusion, and eroding through the skull base foramina to involve cranial nerves and the cavernous sinus. Its rich lymphatic drainage leads to early and often bilateral cervical lymph node metastasis, and distant spread to bone, lung and liver can occur.
additionalDifferentials: Lymphoma of the nasopharynx or neck
Other nasopharyngeal tumours such as minor salivary gland tumours
additionalInvestigations: Nasopharyngeal endoscopy with biopsy of any suspicious lesion
MRI of the nasopharynx and skull base to assess local and perineural extension
CT to evaluate bony erosion and nodal disease
PET-CT for staging and detection of distant metastases
Epstein-Barr virus serology and plasma EBV DNA levels
Fine needle aspiration of a neck node when the primary is not yet identified
Audiometry and tympanometry to document middle ear effusion
redFlags: Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult, which mandates nasopharyngeal examination to exclude this tumour
A persistent painless neck mass, especially in the upper deep cervical chain
Cranial nerve palsies, diplopia or facial numbness suggesting skull base invasion
Trismus, persistent headache or unexplained weight loss
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on stage at presentation; early disease treated with radiotherapy has a favourable prognosis, whereas advanced disease with skull base invasion or distant metastasis carries a poorer outlook, and the frequently late presentation makes vigilance for early signs important.
pitfalls: Treating adult unilateral middle ear effusion as simple Eustachian tube dysfunction without examining the nasopharynx
Attributing a neck node to benign causes and delaying evaluation of the primary
Taking an inadequate or superficial biopsy of a submucosal tumour
Underestimating skull base and perineural spread by relying on CT alone rather than MRI
Overlooking cranial nerve findings as unrelated
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
